title: Erdős #635 OQ-01: Near-Uniqueness of Maximum 1-Admissible Sets
description: In any maximum 1-admissible set in {1,...,N}, every element strictly less than N must be odd. The odd set is 'almost unique' as an optimizer — the only possible non-odd element is N itself. For odd N, the odd set is the unique maximum. 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: This result extends the Erdős #635 formalization by characterizing the extremal structure beyond just the cardinality bound. The parent file proved f(N,1) = (N+1)/2 (the odd set is optimal), but left open whether other maximum sets exist. This OQ answers that question: the odd set is essentially unique, with the only possible variation at the boundary element N.
overview.problemStatement:
**Result:** In any maximum 1-admissible set $A \subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $|A| = \lfloor(N+1)/2\rfloor$, every element $a \in A$ with $a < N$ satisfies $a \equiv 1 \pmod{2}$.

**Corollaries:**
- For odd $N$: the odd set is the unique maximum
- For any $N$: at most one even element (only $N$ itself)
overview.text: Characterizes the structure of maximum 1-admissible sets: all interior elements must be odd, with at most one even element possible at the boundary.
overview.proofStrategy: **Fiber partition argument.** The injection $\varphi(a) = \lfloor(a-1)/2\rfloor$ partitions $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ into fibers $\{2v+1, 2v+2\}$. A maximum set picks exactly one from each fiber. If any non-last fiber picks its even element $2v+2$, both elements of the next fiber are blocked: $(2v+3) - (2v+2) = 1$ divides everything, and $(2v+4) - (2v+2) = 2$ divides $2v+4$. Missing a fiber contradicts maximality.
keyInsights: **Fiber blocking**: An even element blocks both elements of the next fiber — the odd neighbor by difference 1, the even neighbor by difference 2 dividing an even number
**Near-uniqueness**: The odd set is the unique maximum for all odd N and 'almost all' even N, with the only alternative at the boundary
**Structural rigidity**: The injection argument shows the odd numbers aren't just one optimizer among many — they're essentially the only one

conclusion.summary: The odd set {1, 3, 5, ...} is essentially the unique maximum 1-admissible set in {1,...,N}. Every element strictly below N must be odd in any maximum set, and the only possible deviation is at the boundary element N itself. For odd N, the odd set is the unique optimizer.
conclusion.implications: This structural characterization goes beyond the cardinality result f(N,1) = (N+1)/2 from the parent file. It reveals that the extremal problem has a rigid solution: the odd numbers aren't just one example, they're essentially the only example. This kind of uniqueness result is valuable in extremal combinatorics, as it shows the optimizer is robust.
openQuestions: For even N that are powers of 2 (e.g., N=8), the alternative set {1,3,...,N-3,N} is also maximum. Can we fully characterize which even N admit this alternative?
For t = 2, are the extremal sets similarly structured? The additional freedom (consecutive elements allowed) may create more optima.
